items.title: Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers
items.summary: Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills.And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state. Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock? For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month.Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it?The TL;DR on WatchersWatchers keeps an eye on one things you care about, such as a service, a dependency, or a fix you shipped after an incident. Think of it as the dashboard check you'd otherwise do by hand, done around the clock. It stays quiet until something needs attention, then it sends you its assessment and the evidence behind it. For critical findings, it can also launch an Investigation in Assistant to find the cause.Here's the gist of how it helps you identify potential issues in a cost-effective manner, which I'll cover in greater detail in the remaining sections in this post:The design: A capable agent calibrates each watcher once, so every run after that is plain code plus one call to a small, fast model.The cost: Less than $10 a month per watcher for 41 of our 43 internal Watchers. Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026, and then will bill as part of Assistant token usage.The results: Coverage beyond your alerts, so you catch what you didn’t know to watch for and better trust your system. Our own watcher found more than 10 customer-affecting production bugs in the past few months.The integrations: Watchers read most of your telemetry, plus any HTTP API, and send findings to Slack, Microsoft Teams, webhooks, or Grafana Alerting.Put the intelligence only where it's neededKeeping an eye on a service comes down to three jobs: Working out what to watch and what normal looks likeComparing the same signals with normal again and againDeciding whether anything is worth interrupting someone forOnly the first and last jobs need intelligence, and they need it in very different amounts. Let's go back to our example from the intro about a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes. Determining what to watch takes exploration and judgment, but once you've made a decision, you don't need to revisit it constantly. After all, the answer barely changes between 9 and 9:10 a.m. And deciding whether something matters enough to interrupt someone takes judgment on every run, but it's a narrow question once the legwork is done. The middle job is fetching data and doing arithmetic, which code does well and LLMs don't. So a watcher splits the work three ways:JobWho does itWhenDecide what to watch and what normal looks likeA calibration agent, with a capable model and toolsOnce, and again when you recalibrateFetch the data and compare it with the baselinePlain code: queries, statistics, and log pattern trackingEvery runDecide whether it matters, and explain whyA small, fast model, in a single call with no toolsEvery runAnd here's what that workflow looks like:Calibration: do the hard thinking onceCalibration is the secret sauce. Think of it as pre-processing: when you create a watcher, a background agent does the setup work an experienced engineer would normally do and writes down what it learns. The expensive reasoning happens once, and every run inherits a narrow, well-prepared task that an LLM is good at.The calibration agent:Settles the scope. It maps where your telemetry lives and asks you up front when it hits a question that only you can answer. For example: "This service runs in 32 production clusters and one ops cluster. Should each cluster be judged on its own?"Starts from what your team knows. It mines your alert rules and dashboards first, since they encode failure modes, thresholds, and severities your team already agreed on.Measures normal over time.
